extracted.intended_audience: artists, manga fans, and students/researchers interested in shoujo manga history and visual style
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and descriptive criteria for the visual features, historical influences, and decade-by-decade evolution of the shoujo manga / shoujo-illustration art style; useful for evaluating or reproducing period-appropriate shoujo art. Focuses on visual motifs (eyes, faces, figures, clothing), artistic influences (bijinga, jojouga, youga, nihonga, Art Nouveau), and major practitioners (Nakahara, Takahashi, Takabatake, Year 24 Group).

rubrics_metrics.name: Large, sparkly / exaggerated eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters feature huge, exaggerated eyes with many highlights — often 'sparkly' and sometimes shaped like stars — a salient trait of shoujo manga.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post emphasizes that the hugely exaggerated eyes are a defining shoujo trait and argues their lineage comes from Nakahara and Takahashi (and jojouga traditions) rather than Tezuka/Disney. Example phrasing: 'the use of hugely exaggerated eyes, which are not only large but feature many highlights, often shaped like stars.' When reproducing/evaluating shoujo, check for size, number and shape of highlights and a generally emotive, expressive eye design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facial linework and features (nose, mouth, angles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faces are drawn with narrow, softly-curving lines; noses are represented by a slender dash or subtle curve; mouths are small (a 'bud-mouth'); facial angles are delicate and stylized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author connects these conventions to bijinga/ukiyo-e and to Nakahara Junichi's illustrations. Quoted visual cues: 'The narrow, softly-curving lines of the face, the slender dash and curve that represents a nose in subtle lines, and the small mouth we associate with manga art.' Use these cues to assess authenticity or to render a shoujo face.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figure stylization: willowy, slender, fashion-illustration bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies are often willowy and slender, reminiscent of fashion illustration; face shape and proportions shift by era (rounder for younger characters in the 60s, narrower for mature characters from the 70s onward).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post links figure stylization to target demographics and era: 'willowy, slender figure reminiscent of fashion illustration' and notes round faces in 60s shoujo aimed at elementary-school girls versus 'narrower faces (to denote maturity)' in later decades. Use body proportions and face shape to date or emulate a style period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotive, non-narrative backgrounds and layering
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of emotive backgrounds, non-narrative images, and layered, lyrical elements in page/composition design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributed particularly to Takahashi Macoto: 'pioneered the use of emotive backgrounds, non-narrative images, and layering.' This lyrical, atmospheric approach derives from jojouga and is a hallmark of shoujo visual storytelling; evaluate compositions for background mood and abstract/poetic elements rather than purely literal settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed garments and emphasis on clothing/ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Richly detailed garments, decorative clothing, and an emphasis on fashion/cosmetics aesthetics are central to many shoujo illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes magazine illustrators' commercial roles (department store advertising, cosmetics) and says 'This emphasis on rich, detailed garments translated well to the commercial demands of magazine illustration.' When producing or judging shoujo art, check costume detail and decorative emphasis as a key stylistic marker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Androgyny and sameness; elegantly stylised form
rubrics_metrics.description: A tendency toward androgynous looks and a stylized sameness in figures/faces — elegant, stylised forms rather than individualized realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited from Takabatake Kashou's influence: 'a tendency toward androgyny and sameness that would mark ... girls' magazines and postwar shoujo manga.' This is a compositional and character-design trait to consider when aiming for prewar/postwar magazine authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jojouga (lyrical pictures) influence: sentimental, atmospheric, wispy depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The jojouga tradition brought sentimental, lyrical, and atmospheric depictions of young women — wispy, ephemeral presentations rather than bold realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Yumeji Takehisa 'pioneered the style which came to be known as jojouga (lyrical pictures 叙情画)' and produced work without the wide eyes but with a 'sentimental and atmospheric' feel. This lineage explains shoujo's lyricism; evaluate/produce with emphasis on atmosphere and ephemeral rendering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijinga / ukiyo-e influence (portraits of beautiful women)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linework, small mouths, slender noses and portrait composition draw on bijinga (ukiyo-e portraits of beautiful women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post explicitly connects early shoujo magazine art to ukiyo-e's bijinga: 'The narrow, softly-curving lines... small mouth we associate with manga art are all features of bijinga.' Use bijinga conventions as a visual reference when assessing or creating historically-rooted shoujo art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fusion of Western and Japanese fine-art modes (youga, nihonga, Art Nouveau)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shoujo illustration often synthesizes Western-style painting (youga), Japanese-style painting (nihonga), and Western design movements like Art Nouveau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists like Takabatake Kashou combined 'Western influences, such as Art Nouveau, with nihonga and bijinga' to create a modern shoujo-friendly illustration style. When evaluating authenticity, look for cross-cultural aesthetic elements (line, composition, decorative motifs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Era- and demographic-driven face/figure conventions (60s roundness; 70s maturity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Face and figure conventions change by decade and intended readership: 1960s art often features round faces targeting young girls; 1970s art shifts to narrower faces and more mature, dramatic styling aligned with older protagonists and themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author links demographic targeting and thematic shifts to visible stylistic changes: 'round faces' in the 60s for elementary-school readership; 'narrower faces (to denote maturity)' with the Year 24 Group and 70s works. Use these signals to date or match style to intended audience/era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic influence on style: psychological, sexuality, gender, social issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A shift toward psychological themes, sexuality, gender and social-issue content (notably in the 1970s, e.g., the Year 24 Group) corresponded to a more mature, dramatic art style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post argues the Year 24 Group's thematic innovations caused visual maturation: 'their works were marked by a huge emphasis on psychological themes, sexuality and gender, and social issues... this is also why the art style became more mature and dramatic.' Evaluate whether thematic content and visual style align when judging period pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decadal stylistic evolution and settled 1990s aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize a historical progression: pre-1950s influences → 1950s emergence (Takahashi) → 1960s round-faced youth style → 1970s mature/dramatic shift → 1980s willowy return → 1990s consolidation of a 'settled' shoujo look.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article traces changes across decades and states 'I personally would consider the art style of shoujo to have 'matured' or 'settled' a bit in the 90s.' Use decade-specific markers (face shape, body proportions, background treatment, emotional register) to evaluate or recreate an era-accurate shoujo style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial formats and merchandise shaping style (magazine covers, stationery, postcards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shoujo art was produced for magazines and mass-market goods (covers, stationery, postcards), and this commercial context influenced style choices (decorative detail, reproducibility, formats).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes Yumeji Takehisa and others produced 'stationary, letter sets, and postcards' and that magazine illustrators' commercial roles influenced ornamentation and repeatable motifs. When creating or evaluating shoujo art intended for merchandise, prioritize decorative clarity and repeatable motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of stylistic origins: credit Nakahara Junichi and Takahashi Macoto over Tezuka for shoujo look
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical attribution: the wide-eyed shoujo 'look' and many stylistic features are best ascribed to Nakahara Junichi and later Takahashi Macoto (and jojouga tradition), not solely to Tezuka Osamu or Disney influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post explicitly disputes common English-language claims crediting Tezuka: 'it seems unlikely that an artist who primarily worked in shounen could be responsible for the staple large, sparkly eyes which mark so many shoujo manga.' It advises that Nakahara is 'widely regarded as the inventor of the wide-eyed "manga" looks' and Takahashi popularized emotive backgrounds and layering. Use correct lineage when contextualizing or crediting influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global diffusion and adaptation of shoujo aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Shoujo aesthetics have been adopted and adapted internationally (China, Taiwan, Korea, Latin America, Europe), producing local variants while maintaining core markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes imports and adaptations (manhua, manhwa, Tokyopop's 'International Women of Manga', Italian girls' comics) and suggests shoujo's core visual vocabulary travels globally. When evaluating non-Japanese works labeled 'shoujo', check for core features (eyes, linework, emotive backgrounds, garment detail) and note local inflections.
